But to say that I am untouched by it is a monstrous accusation, Leo. It is simply that I process these things differently. If you had walked in yesterday, just as the evening light was turning the dust motes to gold, you would have found me utterly despondent. I wept, I assure you. Even my man, Travers, who brought me the telegram, had the good sense to withdraw without a word. I experienced the whole ghastly business in a single, perfect hour. Then it was done. I cannot linger in an emotion; it is like holding a single note until it becomes discordant. Only the truly sentimental believe they can sustain a feeling indefinitely.

And you, my dear Leo, are a victim of your own sympathy. You came here to find a wretch, and are incensed to discover a man. It is the paradox of the consoling friend. You remind me of a story Julian told me about a celebrated botanist who spent his life searching for a flower believed to be extinct, a sort of black tulip with a crimson heart. After decades, he found a single specimen in a forgotten Alpine valley. He documented it, painted it, and then, in his moment of triumph, he was miserable. His life’s purpose had vanished into a notebook. He became a recluse and took up an interest in bookkeeping, of all things. And besides, if you genuinely wish to soothe me, do not ask me to feel what is past; ask me instead to see it as a necessary cadence in a larger composition. Was it not Julian who spoke of finding solace in the pure architecture of a melody?

I am not one for trinkets, as you know. I do not find comfort in the weight of a paperweight or the texture of old leather. Silks and velvets are for the senses, but they do not touch the soul. It is the aesthetic temperament itself, the ability to transmute life into art, that offers the only real escape. To become the audience to your own drama, as Julian says, is to be free from the pain of being an actor in it. I know this surprises you. You see me as you saw me at Oxford, a boy scribbling verse and full of earnest passions. I am a man now, Leo. I have new appetites, new philosophies. I am changed, but you must not abandon me. You must always be my friend. Of course, I am devoted to Julian. But you possess a goodness he lacks. You are not as brilliant, perhaps—you are too in awe of the world to mock it properly—but you are better. And we were so happy once, were we not? Do not argue with me, Leo. I am what I am. There is nothing else to be said.”

The older man sighed, the anger draining from his face, replaced by a familiar, weary affection. The boy—for he would always be a boy to him—was precious, and his intellect had been the catalyst for Leo’s own best critical work. He could not bring himself to lecture him further. His callousness was a pose, surely; a mask that would one day be set aside. So much of him was still fine, still true.

“But surely she did?”

“Only Alistair. And I am certain she never spoke it. She told me once her family was terribly inquisitive about me. She said she told them my name was Apollo. It was a charming little fantasy. It is your masterpiece, by your own account. Unlock the case, Alistair. It is a crime for your valet to hide your work away like that. I knew the study felt different when I came in.”

“Do not speak!”

Alistair ran a hand over his brow. It was damp with sweat. He felt he was standing at the edge of a precipice. “You told me a month ago it was not ready,” he cried. “Why have you changed your mind?
